Hi Kimberly,

Thanks again for the demo last week — CardioTech is excited about Redwood’s latency profile for real-time reporting. Procurement asked me to send a formal request for an SLA addendum that covers our specific uptime and 99th percentile inference-latency commitments for the three mission-critical routes we’ll run (patient-reporting, anomaly-detection, and billing-classification).

Can you confirm what evidence you can attach and whether Redwood will agree to a tailored order-form clause for the three routes listed? We’d like to close the procurement review by Dec 10 if possible.

Thanks,

Neha / Rishi — forwarding CardioTech’s request (see attached). Key asks: explicit p99 latency def, uptime evidence, and a tailored order-form clause that binds three specific routes to their tiers. Procurement wants to close by Dec 10; Maria asked for a first-pass by tomorrow EOD.

I attached a quick draft exhibit (redwood-sla-exhibit-draft.docx) — it scopes the three routes and proposes uptime commitments per route: 99.95% monthly for patient-reporting, 99.9% for anomaly-detection, and 99.5% for billing-classification, with typical remedies (service credits) mapped to % of monthly fees.

Please review the following before I send to Maria:
- Neha: confirm the p99 latency definition wording and what metric slice we can commit (e.g., server-side inference time at p99 excluding network and client deserialization). Also list what historical latency sample (csv) we can include.
- Rishi: confirm any operational constraints for the anomaly route that should be reflected (batching, quantization tradeoffs, expected cold-starts) and whether we need a non-standard exclusion for scheduled maintenance windows.

Attachments: redwood-sla-exhibit-draft.docx
From: neha_kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.com>

Kimberly — I reviewed the draft and made the following recommendations (high level):

1) Latency definition: propose exact wording: "Server-side inference latency (p99) measured at the Redwood serving layer from model invocation start to token-output completion, excluding customer-side network transit and client deserialization. Measurements are calculated per-route on a 5-minute sample window and reported as the p99 over a monthly calendar window."

2) Evidence bundle: I can attach our last 90 days of per-route uptime/latency aggregates, the regional failover runbook excerpt, and a short report from our most recent DR test (Oct 2026). Practical filenames I will include: latency-metrics-sample.csv, ops-evidence.zip. Ops evidence contains runbook.pdf and failover-log.txt.

3) Order-form notes: suggest mapping the three routes to distinct tier names (Patient-RT, Detect-High, Billing-Async) so we can control batch/quantization defaults per tier. Also include a clause that scheduled maintenance windows are excluded with 72-hour notice.

I attached the sample csv and a marked-up exhibit draft. If that looks good I’m okay sharing the bundle with CardioTech.

—Neha
Director, Reliability Engineering
Redwood Inference

Attachments: latency-metrics-sample.csv, ops-evidence.zip, (annotated) redwood-sla-exhibit-draft.docx

Neha / Kimberly — quick operational note from infra: the proposed 99.95% for patient-reporting is plausible for single-region dedicated pools given their RPS, but we should add a short caveat about quantization/throughput tradeoffs on the anomaly-detection route. Specifically: if the customer requires lower-bit quantization to maintain latency at scale, we may need to reserve a small buffer for peak concurrency or require a burst-capacity plan in the order form.

Also recommend we define what constitutes an "urgent remediation window" vs standard SLA investigation window (48 hours vs 5 business days) so procurement understands response expectations.

I don’t object to the tier mapping Neha suggested; will add a one-paragraph ops note to the exhibit.

—Rishi
